content.title: About
content.content: A classic dish featuring tender beef, boiled or roasted potatoes, and a mix of vegetables – carrots, broccoli and dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale). Served with a savory gravy that ties all components together.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef is one of the most widely consumed sources of animal protein worldwide.
Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century and have become a staple food.
Broccoli belongs to the cruciferous family, along with cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Dark‑green leafy vegetables provide high amounts of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Beef supplies all essential amino acids needed for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef is a good source of B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Potassium and magnesium
items.content: Potatoes and leafy greens are rich in potassium, which helps regulate blood pressure, while magnesium supports muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Broccoli and carrots contain vitamin C and carotenoids that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and potatoes (especially with skin) provide fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Saturated fat intake
items.content: Fatty cuts of beef can raise cholesterol levels if consumed excessively.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies often contain high salt; monitor the amount added.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Rare, but some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to beef.

items.title: Potential pathogens
items.content: Undercooked beef may harbor bacteria such as E. coli or salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of at least 63 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice beef into bite‑size pieces and sear or braise until tender. Boil, bake, or roast potatoes. Steam, blanch or lightly sauté carrots, broccoli and greens to retain crunch and nutrients. Drizzle the gravy over the assembled plate just before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh beef refrigerated at +2–4 °C for 3–5 days or freeze at ‑18 °C for up to 6 months. Store potatoes in a cool, dark place and vegetables in the fridge in airtight containers. Gravy should be kept in a sealed jar in the refrigerator and used within 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Meatless chicken is a plant‑based substitute for chicken fillet made from soy protein, wheat gluten and flavorings. The product is coated with breadcrumbs and deep‑fried, giving it a crispy golden crust that mimics traditional fried chicken.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product is completely plant‑based but designed to taste and feel like real chicken.
Whole‑grain breadcrumbs are often used for the coating, adding extra fiber.
Deep‑frying creates a crunchy exterior but also increases the calorie count.
Fortified versions may contain B‑vitamins to resemble the nutritional profile of real meat.
Suitable for vegetarians, but not vegans if egg is used in the breading.

items.title: High in plant protein
items.content: Soy protein provides a complete amino‑acid profile that supports muscle maintenance and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with traditional fried chicken, the product contains less saturated fat when cooked in vegetable oil.

items.title: Source of iron and zinc
items.content: Fortified versions can supply essential minerals that aid immune function and metabolism.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain breading adds fiber, which promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Cholesterol‑free
items.content: Plant‑based substitutes contain no cholesterol, benefiting cardiovascular health.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: People with soy allergy may experience mild to severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie content when fried
items.content: Deep‑frying adds significant calories and fat, so portion control is important.

items.title: Contains glutamate
items.content: Monosodium glutamate is often added for flavor and may be problematic for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Not vegan
items.content: If egg is used in the breading, the product is not suitable for vegans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a main dish with vegetables, potatoes or rice, add to salads, sandwiches or tacos. Preheat oil to 180 °C, fry until golden, then let excess oil drain before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed package in the refrigerator at 0 °C‑4 °C for up to 5 days. Frozen version stores up to 3 months at –18 °C. Discard if it develops a rancid oil smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Plain corn chips are crispy slices made from whole‑grain corn flour, fried or baked to a golden crunch. They contain no added flavors, preserving the natural corn taste. Chips are commonly enjoyed as a snack with dips, as a side for meals, or simply on their own.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn chips originated in the United States in the early 1900s and quickly became popular for their simplicity and long shelf life.
Traditional chips are produced from dry corn flour that undergoes extrusion, giving them their characteristic shape and texture.
Plain chips are often used in Mexican cuisine as a base for dishes like nachos or as a crunchy topping for soups.
Corn, the base ingredient, is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Compared with potato chips, plain corn chips usually contain less sodium when no extra salt is added.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Corn chips provide steady energy through slowly digestible carbs, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain versions supply a modest amount of fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Low in trans fats
items.content: When fried in non‑hydrogenated oil, the chips contain little to no trans fatty acids.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Corn contains carotenoids and phenolic compounds that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Corn chips are suitable for people with gluten intolerance, provided no wheat‑based additives are used.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Some plain chips are heavily salted, which can be problematic for individuals with hypertension.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Chips are energy‑dense; overconsumption may contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: Trans fats from improper frying
items.content: If chips are fried in hydrogenated oils, they may contain trans fats that increase cardiovascular risk.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy plain corn chips as a snack, with salsa, guacamole, cheese dip, or use them as a crunchy base for casseroles, salads, and soups.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep chips in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For extended freshness, store them in the refrigerator to prevent fat oxidation.

meatballs-swedish-in-gravy-with-noodles-.title: Swedish Meatballs in Gravy with Noodles

content.title: About
content.content: Swedish meatballs in gravy with noodles is a diet-friendly frozen meal designed for quick, balanced nutrition. The package includes small meatballs in a creamy gravy served over cooked noodles, providing a complete portion for 1‑2 meals with a balanced mix of protein, carbs, and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional Swedish meatballs are made from a blend of beef and pork seasoned with nutmeg and allspice.
The gravy is a reduction of cream and broth, giving it a smooth, velvety texture.
The noodles are typically short egg noodles that cook quickly in the microwave.
The dish became popular in the United States in the 1950s as part of the “Ready‑to‑Eat” convenience food movement.
Freezing the meal preserves nutrients without the need for artificial preservatives.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: The meatballs provide high‑quality animal protein essential for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Balanced carbohydrates
items.content: Noodles supply complex carbs for sustained energy and help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Low in added sugars
items.content: The meal contains no added sugars, making it suitable for low‑sugar diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and gravy contain B12, B6, and niacin, supporting metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The creamy gravy adds a modest amount of calcium and vitamin D, beneficial for bone health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The gravy contains cream, so individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should avoid it.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared meals can be high in salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Proper heating required
items.content: Insufficient heating may leave harmful bacteria; follow microwave instructions carefully.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: The creamy sauce adds saturated fat, which should be considered by people watching cholesterol levels.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Microwave the meal according to the package directions, stir the meatballs with gravy and noodles, and let stand for 1‑2 minutes. Serve hot, optionally garnished with fresh herbs or a pinch of black pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the frozen product at –18 °C or lower. Once thawed, consume within 24 hours and store in the refrigerator for no more than 2 days. Discard if the packaging is damaged or the product develops an off‑odor.

rice-brown-with-carrots-and-tomatoes-and.title: Brown Rice with Carrots and Tomatoes

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains the bran and germ layers. In this dish the rice is cooked with carrots, tomatoes and/or a tomato‑based sauce, with added fat, making it more flavorful and nutritionally dense.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice retains more fiber, vitamins, and minerals than white rice.
Carrots are rich in beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A.
Tomatoes contain lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that supports cell health.
Adding a small amount of fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from tomatoes.
The dish can be easily adapted to various cuisines by swapping the tomato sauce for a paste or adding different spices.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Brown rice provides dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Carrots supply beta‑carotene, supporting vision and immune function.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Lycopene from tomatoes helps combat free radicals and may reduce the risk of chronic diseases.

items.title: Heart‑friendly fats
items.content: The added healthy fats improve cholesterol levels and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Steady energy source
items.content: Complex carbohydrates in rice release glucose slowly, providing sustained energy.

items.title: Calorie density
items.content: The added fat increases the dish’s calorie count, so portion control is important for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may be allergic to rice, experiencing skin or gastrointestinal reactions.

items.title: Oxalate content
items.content: Tomatoes contain oxalates, which in excess can contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve as a side dish with meat, fish, or legumes, incorporate into salads, casseroles, or use as a base for vegetarian meals. Fresh herbs, spices, or a squeeze of lemon can enhance the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑sized bags – the flavor and nutrients remain intact.
